library, launch checklist 1. Executive summary The situation BrightChamps  is doubling down on one market and one subject:  the USA and Math . Two things must improve every month: the  quantity  of leads and the  quality  of leads. Today the blended cost per lead (CPL) is  $50 . The goal is  $25 , which means the same media budget must buy roughly twice as many leads, or the same number of leads must cost half as much. The thesis CPL is not one number to push on. It is the output of three levers, each owned by a different team: <w:tblPr><w:tblW w:w="9360" w:type="dxa"/><w:tblBorders><w:top w:val="single" w:sz="4" w:space="0" w:color="auto"/><w:left w:val="single" w:sz="4" w:space="0" w:color="auto"/><w:bottom w:val="single" w:sz="4" w:space="0" w:color="auto"/><w:right w:val="single" w:sz="4" w:space="0" w:color="auto"/><w:insideH w:val="single" w:sz="4" w:space="0" w:color="auto"/><w:insideV w:val="single" w:sz="4" w:space="0" w:color="auto"/></w:tblBorders><w:tblCellMar><w:left w:w="10" w:type="dxa"/><w:right w:w="10" w:type="dxa"/></w:tblCellMar><w:tblLook w:val="0000" w:firstRow="0" w:lastRow="0" w:firstColumn="0" w:lastColumn="0" w:noHBand="0" w:noVBand="0"/></w:tblPr><w:tblGrid><w:gridCol w:w="9360"/></w:tblGrid><w:tr w:rsidR="00C97AED" w14:paraId="0BA8A1F1" w14:textId="77777777"><w:tblPrEx><w:tblCellMar><w:top w:w="0" w:type="dxa"/><w:bottom w:w="0" w:type="dxa"/></w:tblCellMar></w:tblPrEx><w:trPr><w:cantSplit/></w:trPr><w:tc><w:tcPr><w:tcW w:w="9360" w:type="dxa"/><w:tcBorders><w:top w:val="none" w:sz="0" w:space="0" w:color="FFFFFF"/><w:left w:val="single" w:sz="36" w:space="0" w:color="00BAF2"/><w:bottom w:val="none" w:sz="0" w:space="0" w:color="FFFFFF"/><w:right w:val="none" w:sz="0" w:space="0" w:color="FFFFFF"/></w:tcBorders><w:shd w:val="clear" w:color="auto" w:fill="E6F7FE"/><w:tcMar><w:top w:w="120" w:type="dxa"/><w:left w:w="200" w:type="dxa"/><w:bottom w:w="120" w:type="dxa"/><w:right w:w="160" w:type="dxa"/></w:tcMar></w:tcPr><w:p w14:paraId="52E4D0F1" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00C97AED" w:rsidRDefault="00000000"><w:pPr><w:spacing w:after="60"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:rPr><w:b/><w:bCs/><w:color w:val="002E6E"/></w:rPr><w:t>CPL = CPM ÷ (1,000 × CTR × Landing-page CVR) CPM  (cost to be seen) and  CTR  (share of viewers who click) are the  marketing engine . 2025 benchmark median for its lever (Meta CTR median about 2.19%, education landing-page conversion median about 5.7%). The plan does not need heroic execution on any one lever. It needs three ordinary improvements to land together. The guardrail Halving CPL is easy if quality is allowed to fall: loosen targeting, buy junk traffic, and $25 arrives while the business quietly breaks. Every recommendation here therefore travels with a  lead-quality index  that must stay at or above 100 (baseline). A relative drop of more than 15% in lead-to-paid conversion pauses the responsible lever. The mathematical limit is generous, because halving CPL leaves room for quality to fall by up to 50% before cost per paid student worsens, but the plan uses a far tighter tripwire on purpose (Section 8). What success looks like Month 1:  CPL about $43 from quick wins (form cut, creative refresh).  Month 3:  about $30.  Month 5:  $25.  Month 12:  about $20 with audience expansion working (commit $25, stretch $20). At constant $100K monthly media budget:  leads rise from about 2,000 to about 4,000 per month.  At constant lead volume:  $50K per month of media budget is released. Cost per paid student  (media only, illustrative funnel) falls from about  $712  to about  $356  if lead quality holds. Decisions requested Approve a  Week 0 measurement audit  so illustrative baselines are replaced with account actuals. Approve  landing-page and booking-flow capacity  (design, front-end, analytics) for a rolling experiment program. Ring-fence an  8% test reserve  of media budget for new formats and audience segments. Adopt the  guardrail and kill rules  in Sections 8 and 14 as standing policy. lever 3. The unit-economics model 3.1 From impressions to leads For any spend S, impressions = S ÷ CPM × 1,000, clicks = impressions × CTR, and leads = clicks × CVR. Dividing spend by leads gives  CPL = CPM ÷ (1,000 × CTR × CVR) . CPL falls when CPM falls, and it falls just as much when CTR or CVR rises by the same proportion. That symmetry is why the plan pulls both engines together rather than betting on one. 3.2 Baseline calibration The stated baseline is a $50 blended CPL. The three inputs below reproduce it exactly, and each is defensible against published 2025 benchmarks. They are illustrative until Week 0 replaces them with account data. <w:tblPr><w:tblW w:w="9360" w:type="dxa"/><w:tblBorders><w:top w:val="single" w:sz="4" w:space="0" w:color="auto"/><w:left The grid shows CPL at CPM of $18 across CTR and CVR values. Any cell shaded green is at or below $25. Note how many combinations work: the target does not depend on a single lever landing perfectly. Figure 2. CPL sensitivity to CTR and landing-page CVR at CPM of $18. Minimum viable path:  CTR 1.6% (no creative gain at all) still reaches $25 if CVR reaches 4.5%. CTR 1.8% needs CVR 4.0%. CTR 2.2% needs only CVR 3.3%. Asymmetry to exploit:  landing-page CVR is fully within  BrightChamps ' control and can be tested within days. CTR and CPM depend partly on auction dynamics. Prioritize CVR early because it is the faster and more reliable lever. Warning cell:  CTR 2.2% with CVR 2.5% still costs $32.70. Better creative that does not convert is the most common way to feel busy without moving CPL. 3.5 Audience mix effect Audience expansion is  modeled  as a second campaign with its own economics: CPM 15% lower, CTR 25% higher and CVR 10% higher than the core plan, reflecting less contested inventory and higher category affinity. These multipliers are  hypotheses to be tested , not facts (Section 7 gives pessimistic and optimistic ranges). trials 4.3 Capacity check before choosing Option A Twice the leads  means  about twice the trial classes, twice the reminders and twice the follow-up calls. Before scaling volume, answer four questions: How many trial slots can teachers deliver per week in each US time zone? How many leads can one representative contact within five minutes and within one hour? What is the no-show recovery process? What is the cost of a trial class (teacher time)? If any answer says capacity is fixed, choose Option C and reinvest released budget in quality improvements, not volume. 5. Marketing engine playbook The marketing engine controls CPM and CTR. The plan needs CPM down about 10% ($20 to $18) and CTR up about 12.5% (1.6% to 1.8%). The test reserve stays at 4% permanently so new ideas always have funding. server-side events  (Meta Conversions API, Google enhanced conversions and offline import) for booked, attended and paid. Without them, platforms optimize on the cheapest clicks, which is exactly the quality trap. Optimize for booked trials first , then move to qualified events when an ad set produces roughly 50 events per week. Below that volume, deeper events starve the algorithm. At most two qualification questions appear before booking, and both must change how the lead is routed. 6.4 Speed, mobile and technical hygiene Largest  contentful  paint under 2.5 seconds on mid-range phones.  Compress images, defer scripts, remove pop-ups. Most paid social traffic is mobile. One-thumb forms:  numeric keypad for phone, autofill for name and email, inline error messages, no captcha unless bot traffic is proven. Message match:  one page variant per ad group, with dynamic headline text where needed, so the promise in the ad is the first thing seen on the page. Human fallback:  click-to-call or text option for parents who prefer to talk, subject to consent rules. Event tracking:  page view, form start, step completion, slot selection, booking confirmation, each with the ad and creative identifier. 6.5 Confirmation and reminder cadence Show rate is a quality metric and a cost metric: every trial no-show wastes a teacher slot and a paid lead. sensitivity grid in Section 3.4 shows that a modest CTR gain closes the rest. Segment-specific pages (T12) are additional upside for expansion audiences and are not counted here. 7. Audience expansion 7.1 Why expand, and why now A single broad audience saturates: frequency rises, CTR falls and CPM climbs. Expansion audiences add fresh inventory, and some carry higher affinity for structured supplemental math. Two anchors from public data (approximate, US Census and Pew Research  Center ): Indian-Americans: about 5.2 to 5.5 million people , with the highest median household income of any major US ethnic group (about $145,000 to $151,000). Small, high-fit and concentrated in a few metros. Hispanic and Latino population: about 62 to 63 million (about 19% of the US) , with a young age profile and the fastest-growing under-18 cohort. Large and currently thin in premium math edtech advertising. Population size is not the same as addressable demand. Household income, grade-age children, digital reach and willingness to pay for live online tutoring shrink the number quickly. restrict direct targeting by ethnicity or other sensitive attributes.  Reach communities through language, geography, permitted interests, lookalikes, community partners and, above all, creative that resonates. Verify current platform policy before launch. Do not stereotype.  Segments are hypotheses about affinity, not assumptions about individuals. Let performance data, not assumptions, decide where budget goes. Fit the product, not just the ad.  A Spanish-language ad that lands on an English-only page with no Spanish-speaking rep wastes the click. Use partners for trust.  Teachers, community organizations and creators from the community carry credibility that paid media cannot buy. 7.4 Localization playbook <w:tblPr><w:tblW w:w="9360" w:type="dxa"/><w:tblBorders><w:top Measure  incremental  leads: expansion should add leads, not relabel leads the core would have found anyway. A geographic holdout is the cleanest test. 8. Lead quality and the guardrail 8.1 The lead-quality index Quality is defined by what happens after the lead, not by how the lead looks. before the business is worse off. Using the illustrative funnel (7.02% of leads become paid students), baseline media cost per paid student is about $712. If CPL falls to $25 but the lead-to-paid rate falls by a fraction d, cost per paid student is $25 ÷ (0.0702 x  (1 - d)). It only matches baseline when d reaches  50% . 8.6 The handoff to sales and onboarding Lead quality is a joint result of marketing and the team that calls the lead. A 5-minute response rule is meaningless if the queue is longer than the day. Capacity formula:  representatives needed = daily leads x average contact minutes per lead ÷ productive minutes per representative per day. At 4,000 leads per month (about 133 per business day), with 6 contact minutes per lead and 300 productive minutes per representative, about 3 representatives are needed for first contact alone, before follow-up. Tag every unqualified lead with a reason  (wrong grade, not interested, unreachable, price). Review reasons weekly with marketing. This is the fastest source of targeting and creative fixes. Share one dashboard.  Marketing sees show and paid rates by campaign; sales  sees  CPL and lead scores by campaign. Neither team optimizes in the dark. 9. Scenario analysis A plan that only works in one world is a forecast, not a plan. This section stress-tests the numbers across ten scenarios, gives a best, base and worst case, and lists what to do when each trigger appears. 9.1 Ten scenarios Figure 9. engine alone reaches $25.  Product-only lands at about $31 and marketing-only at $40. The plan needs both, which is why owners must share one weekly review. Creative that does not convert is the costliest illusion.  A CTR of 2.2% with an unchanged landing page still costs $32.70. Expansion under-delivery is survivable.  If segments perform 10% worse than the core, the blended result is about $26, close to target, not a disaster. Seasonality alone can erase the gain.  A 25% CPM spike moves the core plan to about $31. This is why the calendar in Section 5.6 shifts spend toward retargeting and search in Q4. Scale has a price.  Doubling budget with modest diminishing returns lands near $32, so scale should come from new channels and segments as much as from more spend. 9.2 Best, base and worst case at a $100,000 monthly KPI framework Forty-five metrics sounds like too many. It is not, if each has an owner, a cadence and a threshold that triggers action. Metrics are grouped so that a weekly review can read a handful of headline numbers and drill into a group only when a headline moves. Sources and benchmark notes Figures are approximate, drawn from public sources in 2025 to 2026, and should be re-verified before use in any external document. Meta advertising benchmarks (2025):  platform-wide medians for CPM (about $13 to $14 overall, up to about $20.70 in competitive verticals) and CTR (about 2.19%) as reported in benchmark analyses by Triple Whale and  Influee . These skew toward e-commerce accounts. Landing-page conversion benchmarks:   Unbounce  Conversion Benchmark Report (lead-generation average about 11.9%; education median about 5.7%; all-industry averages roughly 3 to 4%). Indian-American population and income:  Pew Research  Center  analyses of US Census data (about 5.2 to 5.5 million people; median household income about $145,000 to $151,000). Hispanic and Latino population and growth:  US Census Bureau estimates, with purchasing-power and growth analyses from Claritas and  MarketingCharts  (about 62 to 63 million, roughly 19% of the US population). Platform guidance:  Google Stitch, Meta and Google advertising policies should be re-read at launch, because rules on targeting, education claims and minors change frequently. Appendix D. Creative hook library (angles to test) These are angles, not scripts. Each must be produced with real, substantiated stories and consent. Homework night that used to end in tears now ends in questions. A child explains fractions to a parent using a pizza, guided by a live teacher. The difference between doing math and understanding math, shown in 20 seconds. Three signs a child is ready for the next math level. What state-test season really needs: confidence, not cramming. A teacher solves a contest-style problem in a way school rarely shows. Why small live groups beat recorded videos for math. A parent's five-minute check for math gaps at home. Summer slide: how a few weeks of math practice protects a whole year. Before and after: a learner's diagnostic over eight weeks. Bilingual math  help  for families who want both languages in the room. From drive-to- center  to learn-from-anywhere: what a week looks like. Appendix E.
